title: RAG in Java: splitters, fusion and retrieval metrics
seriesDescription: Retrieval metrics, eval gates and guardrail code in Java. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Java code for RAG: LangChain4j splitters, reciprocal rank fusion, recall@k, MRR and nDCG methods, cosine similarity and the arithmetic of chunks and vectors.
source: LangChain4j 1.23 compiled and run locally; Cormack et al. RRF paper (SIGIR 2009); Manning, Raghavan, Schutze: Introduction to Information Retrieval

questions.prompt: Write a Java method static List<String> rrf(List<List<String>> rankings, int k) where each inner list holds document ids, best first. Return the ids sorted by fused reciprocal rank fusion score (sum of 1 / (k + rank) with ranks starting at 1), highest score first.
questions.explanation: The loop index is 0-based, so rank = i + 1. I compiled and ran it with two rankings. Other solutions pass: a `TreeMap`, an explicit comparator, or a stream collector. Ties are broken arbitrarily unless you add a secondary key. LangChain4j ships `ReciprocalRankFuser` for Content lists.

questions.prompt: Write two Java methods: static double recallAtK(List<String> retrieved, Set<String> relevant, int k) returning the fraction of the relevant ids found in the first k retrieved ids, and static double mrr(List<List<String>> retrieved, List<Set<String>> relevant) returning the mean reciprocal rank of the first relevant hit per query (0 for a miss).

checks.label: looks only at the first k
divides by the relevant count without integer division
adds 1 / rank of the first hit

questions.explanation: Casting before the division matters: hits / `relevant.size()` with two ints truncates to 0 or 1. On the three-query example from the retrieval-metrics quiz this returns an MRR of 0.5. Guard an empty relevant set in real code.

questions.prompt: Write `static double ndcgAtK(double[] rels, int k)` where `rels` holds the graded relevance of the retrieved documents in rank order. DCG sums `rel / log2(position + 1)` over the first `k` results; divide by the DCG of the same scores sorted best first. Return 0 when the ideal DCG is 0.
questions.explanation: Java has no log2, so divide natural logs. The position is i + 1, giving `log2(i + 2)`. I ran `ndcgAtK(new double[]{1, 0, 1}, 3)` and got 0.9197, the 92 from the metrics integer question. Arrays.sort is ascending, hence the manual reverse.

questions.prompt: Write static double cosine(double[] a, double[] b) for two equal-length vectors: the dot product divided by the product of the two Euclidean norms.

checks.label: takes square roots for the norms

questions.explanation: I ran `cosine(new double[]{3, 4}, new double[]{4, 3})` and got 0.96. A zero vector divides by zero (`NaN`), so guard it. For L2-normalised embeddings the norms are 1 and the dot product alone equals the cosine.

The loop starts are 0, 400, 800, 1200, 1600 and 2000, so there are 6 chunks. The last holds only 100 characters, all of them already inside the previous chunk's overlap. I ran it; with 2,000 characters the same loop gives 5.

questions.prompt: A float[1000][1536] array holds 1,000 embeddings of 1,536 dimensions. Ignoring array headers, how many bytes do the float values themselves occupy?
questions.explanation: 1,000 x 1,536 x 4 bytes (a Java float is 4 bytes) = 6,144,000 bytes, about 6.1 MB. A million vectors is 1,000 times that, roughly 6.1 GB before any index overhead.

questions.prompt: A teammate's RRF ends with `scores.entrySet().stream().sorted(Map.Entry.comparingByValue()).map(Map.Entry::getKey).toList()` and the worst documents come back first. What is the bug?

options.text: `comparingByValue()` sorts ascending, so the comparator must be reversed.
options.why: Right: .`reversed()` or a reverse-order comparator puts the highest fused score first.

options.text: Map.Entry cannot be compared by value, so the entries must be copied into an array first.
options.why: `Map.Entry.comparingByValue()` works for Comparable values such as Double.

options.text: The score should be multiplied by the rank, so that higher ranks sort to the end of the list.
options.why: RRF adds 1 / (k + rank) per list; multiplying by the rank would reverse the intent.

options.text: `toList()` returns the scores instead of the document ids in this stream pipeline.
options.why: The map step already extracted the keys, so the list holds document ids.

questions.explanation: `Map.Entry.<String, Double>comparingByValue().reversed()` needs the explicit type witness for the call chain to compile, or use `Comparator.comparing(Map.Entry<String, Double>::getValue).reversed()`.

questions.prompt: A `recallAtK` method returns `0.0` for a query where 2 of the 3 relevant documents were retrieved. The last line is `return hits / relevant.size();` with `int hits`. What is the bug?

options.text: Both operands are int, so integer division gives 0 before the result is widened to double.
options.why: Right: 2 / 3 is 0 in integer arithmetic; cast one operand first, for example (double) hits.

options.text: `relevant.size()` returns a long, so the division loses its low-order bits in this expression.
options.why: `size()` returns an int, so no long arithmetic is involved.

options.text: A double result cannot be returned from a method that has an int parameter named k.
options.why: A method's parameter types have no effect on its return type.

options.text: hits was counted before sorting the retrieved list, so the numerator is smaller than expected.
options.why: Recall does not depend on the order of the retrieved ids, only on membership.

questions.explanation: I printed 2 / 3 and got 0. Writing hits / (double) `relevant.size()` or 1.0 * hits / `relevant.size()` fixes it. This is a classic Java trap in metric code.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: For two L2-normalised float vectors a and b, the dot product of a and b equals their cosine similarity.
questions.reason: The norm of a normalised vector is 1, so the denominator of the cosine formula is 1.

whys.a: Both true, and R explains A: with both norms equal to 1 the formula reduces to the dot product.
whys.b: Not chosen: R is exactly why the formula simplifies.
whys.c: Not chosen: R is true, because normalising divides a vector by its length.
whys.d: Not chosen: A is true, since the dot product of unit vectors is the cosine.

questions.explanation: I checked it: (3, 4)/5 dotted with (4, 3)/5 gives 0.96, the same as the cosine of the raw vectors.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence about LangChain4j splitters.
questions.text: DocumentSplitters.{1}(500, 50) builds a splitter that tries paragraphs, then lines, sentences and words, and finally {2}; its split(Document) method returns a List of {3}.
questions.explanation: The result objects are `TextSegments` carrying text and metadata, ready for an `EmbeddingModel`; I compiled the call against LangChain4j 1.23.

questions.prompt: Match each LangChain4j splitter class with the unit it cuts on.
questions.explanation: All four classes exist in LangChain4j 1.23 (I listed them with javap), and `DocumentByCharacterSplitter` is the last-resort cut. They can be chained with a sub-splitter for pieces that are still too long.
